name: Dana Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we run no sales or campaigns. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the clarinet section at a concert hall and teach six private pupils. I warm up before the children leave for school, then go over parts with the woodwinds and play an evening show. I like the moment a student finally finds a clean breath, though late rehearsals make our family timetable a puzzle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who helps keep that timetable together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at the library and handles some pickups, but we check the shift rota every Sunday. We have two children, a mortgage and about ten months of bills saved. I have a master’s in music and good senior fees, but I will not spend the reserve to pretend an unpaid booking is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the woodwinds that a booking form being quicker is welcome, but the concert and lesson still need people. I sometimes use AI to sort rehearsal times, then check the result myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pupils and hall dates are booked this term, and my partner’s library hours are steady. The mortgage takes planning, but ten months saved means ordinary changes do not frighten me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the hall dates and six pupils, put the next term’s fees in writing, and save one fifth of any cleared extra concert fee after mortgage, food and childcare toward twelve months of bills. In the first year of this plateau I would do the same, without buying new software for a small scheduling gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income in this picture. It is the familiar work of getting paid for the hours I have actually booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on the booking form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the fee, rehearsal call and cancellation line against the agreement. A tidy calendar cannot pay a missing rehearsal fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another evening show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the fee covers the extra childcare and travel after the hall’s payment clears. More dates can cost money if I fail to count the pickup.

I would insist on **written fees** for rehearsals and lessons.
think: My **booked hall dates** and six pupils support the mortgage.
Our **ten-month reserve** gives us room for ordinary surprises.
do: Keep **hall dates** and six pupils with written fees this year and through the plateau.
Save **one fifth** of cleared extra concert fees after essentials toward twelve months of bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and family bills in this picture.
S0.quote: A tidy calendar cannot pay a missing rehearsal fee.
fieldNote: Her **written booking terms** matter even when routine software works faster.
A **ten-month reserve** and steady paid hall dates support her calm mood despite a family mortgage.

Save fifth of cleared extra concert fees after mortgage, food and childcare toward twelve months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the booking desk will change before anyone replaces a clarinet on stage. I would ask the hall to show musicians where paid recording and rehearsal work is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some short recording calls and pupil enquiries to go to cheap generated music. Those fees are part of my income, even if my main concert seat is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would count which recording calls disappear and ask the hall for written rates on the remaining ones. If two quarters of paid recording fees fall, I would offer a separate Saturday wind-group clinic only after eight families pay deposits that cover the room, my teaching and preparation, a paid pianist, travel and confirmed childcare; in its first year I would repeat only when the same costs are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real slice of my own pay disappearing. Ten months saved lets me test an answer, but it does not restore a lost fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why eight families?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer fees would leave the pianist or my preparation unpaid after the room charge. Eight deposits are a floor, not a forecast of demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your pupils be entered into an AI booking service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would get families’ permission before putting any pupil details into a tool. I would check every proposed time against my own diary and keep their recordings private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that 2028 thinking AGI could plan and make recordings before any robot can play a stage part around 2031. We should read the next hall contract carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall could buy fewer recording sessions quickly, and a few parents may stop paying for lessons. I still have live work and savings, but the lost fees would touch our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get written hall dates and confirm the six pupils’ next term. In the first year after 2028, if recording calls stop and lesson hours fall, I would seek an advertised conservatory ensemble-lead job only if it accepts my master’s, has paid hours, and gives a written net offer after travel that replaces the lost income with childcare confirmed; I would keep the hall and pupils until I sign that offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about having two years for a pay change. Plenty of nearby music jobs are useful only when one has a real vacancy and an adequate fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a title for less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would count preparation and evening work before signing anything. A grand title does not put money into the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot clarinetist is a later question, around 2031 in this picture. Booking, arranging and recording prices could change in 2028, which is why I would check the contract first.

I would demand **clear hall contracts** before accepting changed fees.

fieldNote: The **2028 pay risk** comes from recordings and lessons, years before robot stage playing.
A **job move** needs a posted qualifying role, written replacement pay and covered childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to see which hall recordings still sell. I would still tell families that live group playing needs listening to one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid recording side may erode by 2031, while a robot player is more a 2034 matter. I could build another paid teaching line, but I will not take a room on faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep the hall and six pupils and ask the pianist whether a separate Saturday clinic suits her. If two quarters of recording income fall, I would run it only after eight paid deposits cover the room, my teaching and preparation, her paid time, travel and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2031 I would continue only while that paid floor holds, keeping hall dates that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the recording side could fade during the next few years. Five years before 2031 lets me find eight families for the Saturday wind clinic, not assume they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who signs for the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sign for one Saturday only after the eight payments clear. The room manager will not absorb my poor guess about demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the pianist just help as a favour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Her rehearsal and teaching time go into the price before I ask her to keep a Saturday free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children that ten years is time to practise and to learn what a paid rehearsal is. Thinking AGI around 2036 and robot players around 2039 are different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still have the clarinet chair, but recorded parts and some lessons may pay less. My partner’s wage and our ten months saved make the next few years sound secure, not the whole decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the hall and six pupils and put one fifth of each cleared extra clinic fee after room, pianist, travel, childcare, mortgage and food toward a twelve-month reserve. Over the decade I would run clinics only after eight deposits pay all those costs and my preparation; in the first year after 2036 I would keep the clinic only if that floor holds, and if hall and lesson fees fall I would seek a posted ensemble-lead job accepting my master’s only with a written net offer after travel replacing the loss and childcare covered, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of recorded music. Our bills are covered now, but I would rather have paid bookings and a reserve than a promise from a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no spare clinic fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing goes into that extra savings pot. I would not count the children’s school money or the mortgage payment as spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sign a longer room lease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual paid Saturday bookings continued to cover it, including the pianist and my preparation. I would start with single dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because recordings and lessons could lose fees before I have time to replace them. I would need honest written hall dates, an actual paid vacancy if I move, and childcare that works on rehearsal nights.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Preparation is part of teaching even when no one hears a note. I will not price the pianist or myself at zero.

headlineQuote: Preparation is part of teaching even when no one hears a note.
portrait: Dana is a **senior clarinet leader** with a music master’s, six pupils and higher fees.
She has a **ten-month reserve**, a library-working partner, two schoolchildren and a mortgage.
She treats **recording losses** as her near-term risk while live playing lasts longer.
She tests **paid clinics** only when deposits cover both musicians, room and childcare.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut recordings and lessons before she replaces their fees.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written hall dates**, a real paid vacancy if moving and workable childcare.
